title: Mail Voting in Turmoil: Your Questions Answered
author: Ask Bolts
content:
Vote-by-mail was not always such a hot topic. It’s a longstanding practice in
the U.S., dating back to the Civil War and even before then. It’s secure, with
audits repeatedly detecting virtually zero fraud. And it’s a very popular
convenience. Every single state and territory permits it on some level.

Everything changed in 2020, when President Trump falsely blamed his election
defeat on voter fraud and subjected mail voting to particular ire, lying to
the public by [calling mail ballots
“fraudulent”](https://www.npr.org/2021/02/08/965342252/timeline-what-trump-
told-supporters-for-months-before-they-attacked) and “a very dangerous thing
for this country.”

Now that he’s back in power, Trump has tried, and so far failed, to command
sweeping election administration changes by executive order, including
proposing severe limits on vote-by-mail access. Republican leaders have
generally fallen in line, in many cases [passing](https://boltsmag.org/utah-
legislation-ending-universal-vote-by-mail/) state-level
[legislation](https://boltsmag.org/ohio-ends-grace-periods-for-mail-ballots/)
that directly answers his calls to restrict mail voting.

Trump issued a sweeping executive order this spring to give the U.S. Postal
Service new authority to refuse to deliver mail ballots in states that don’t
comply with the president’s directives. A federal judge issued her latest
order [blocking these changes on
Thursday](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.mad.298449/gov.uscourts.mad.298449.218.0.pdf),
but they remain subject to a fierce legal battle that Justice Ketanji Brown
Jackson has
[warned](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/26a124_hgci.pdf) may
inject “chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections.”

Separately, voting rights advocates worry that [new USPS rules on
postmarking](https://boltsmag.org/usps-postmark-rules-change-voter-
registration-deadline-election-year/) risk causing a surge in mail ballot
rejections this fall. A third possible disruption to mail voting faltered when
the U.S. Supreme Court in June [rejected](https://boltsmag.org/supreme-court-
allows-grace-periods-for-mail-voting/) a Republican effort to enact a national
ban on so-called grace periods.

We thought you would have many questions on the state of mail voting ahead of
the midterms and so we asked you to send them to us. You all delivered dozens
of queries.

And today, we’re tackling 10 of your questions. Select the one you are most
interested in, or keep scrolling to explore them all.

[What are the new USPS policies?](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#1)

[Are the new rules _legal_?](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#2)

[Are the new rules _feasible_?](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#3)

[What can voters do now?](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#4)

[What if you live overseas?](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#5)

[Who can even get a mail ballot?](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#6)

[What could _states_ do in response?](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#7)

[Do states with an all-mail voting system have a plan
B?](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#8)

[Can you print out your ballot at home?](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#9)

[What is the justification of for these
changes?](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#10)

This is the latest in [our “Ask Bolts”
series](https://boltsmag.org/category/ask-bolts/) where we answer our readers.

**“What are the new USPS policies?” _— @givedogsthevote on Bluesky_**

There are separate issues that have made people nervous about mail ballots
this year.

First: USPS no longer automatically postmarks mail on the day it is received.
Instead, they postmark it when they process it, sometimes after it has
traveled hundreds of miles to a central facility, which can take days.

This matters greatly in states that require mail ballots or voter registration
forms to be postmarked by a certain day to be valid, as [_Bolts_ explained
earlier this year](https://boltsmag.org/usps-postmark-rules-change-voter-
registration-deadline-election-year/). If voters mail their ballots or forms
close to the deadline, USPS may not postmark them in time; the ballots would
then get tossed by election officials.

There’s evidence from primaries held this year that the change is having an
impact; election offices are reporting a [marked
increase](https://www.kqed.org/news/12092639/california-rejected-150000-mail-
ballots-marking-highest-rate-since-2014) in ballots that are rejected because
their postmark is late. In Yakima County, Washington, for instance, roughly 5
percent of mail ballots cast for the Aug. 4 primary were rejected [this
summer](https://www.yakimaherald.com/news/local/government/elections/more-
than-1700-yakima-county-ballots-didnt-meet-postal-deadline-primary-election-
certified/article_925421cf-e4fc-41f5-a62f-e9d90e7df5a9.html), up from 1
percent between 2016 and 2024.

Michelle Kanter Cohen, policy director and senior counsel for the Fair
Elections Center, is afraid that voters are not aware of this issue. “People
have generally assumed that when you put your mail in the official blue box,
that it will be postmarked that day,” she said _._ “But it is clear from this
rule that this is no longer the case.”

The second new USPS policy stems from an [executive
order](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/03/ensuring-
citizenship-verification-and-integrity-in-federal-elections/) that Trump
issued earlier this year.

The order has been blocked by courts for months, and it remains blocked for
now, but USPS [last week released a 95-page rule](https://public-
inspection.federalregister.gov/2026-17238.pdf) that outlines how it intends to
implement Trump’s directive.

The most intrusive requirement is for states to prepare lists of voters who
are eligible to vote by mail and send the lists to the federal government.

The rule says USPS will only deliver mail ballots to people on that list. It
also says it will only deliver ballots with envelopes that meet criteria set
out by the federal government.

USPS says it will refuse to deliver mail ballots to voters in states that do
not comply with the order and do not share lists with the federal government.

Separately, the order directs the Department of Homeland Security and the
Social Security Administration to create a citizenship list to be used by
states to determine who is eligible to vote.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/25085134208474-scaled.jpg)Postal trucks in lower
Manhattan. (Photo by John Lamparski/Sipa USA)

  
**“It sounds like Trump wants the postal service to refuse to deliver some
people 's mail. How can a president do this? Is there any precedent?” — _
Joseph, from Maryland_**

Many election professionals share your assessment and are alarmed by the
administration’s claim that the Postal Service can refuse to deliver some
ballots to individuals who are not on their list.

For now, it seems federal judges agree as well; courts have intervened to stop
the order from taking effect, though a confrontation at the U.S. Supreme Court
likely looms this fall.

Cohen, of the Fair Elections Center, says Trump’s order “would require that
USPS not accept and deliver ballots that it deems out of compliance with the
voter list requirements in the executive order. That is really outrageous,
illegal, and would be unprecedented because the postal service's job is to
accept and deliver mail from every person who mails a mail piece.”

Leah Aden, senior counsel for the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, accused Trump of
“transforming the USPS from a neutral mail carrier to an arbiter of who may
cast a ballot by mail.” She told _Bolts_ , “Federal statutes governing the
USPS do not permit the agency to pick and choose who can vote by mail.”

The executive order is currently facing a series of lawsuits making these and
other arguments.

Democratic officials in 23 states, plus D.C., filed a
[lawsuit](https://www.votebeat.org/national/2026/04/03/donald-
trump-2026-midterm-election-executive-order-state-lawsuit-mail-ballots-josh-
shapiro/) in April, with [another lawsuit](https://lwvofvt.org/lwv-files-
lawsuit-over-mail-voting-executive-order/) filed by the League of Women Voters
and other voting rights organizations. They argue that Trump’s order violates
powers granted by the Constitution for states to administer elections and
determine who is eligible to vote. They also say the order violates the
separation of powers clause by usurping the authority of Congress to make laws
around federal elections.

“This executive order is unlawful and an unprecedented attempt by the federal
government to interfere with how states administer elections,” Celina Stewart,
CEO of the League of Women Voters, told _Bolts_. “The President cannot
override state authority over election administration, and he cannot impose
new election rules by executive order. There is no modern precedent for the
federal government directing USPS to reject mail ballots based on voter
eligibility.”

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, who is overseeing both lawsuits, [issued a
pair of
injunctions](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.mad.298518/gov.uscourts.mad.298518.191.0.pdf)
[this
summer](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.mad.298449/gov.uscourts.mad.298449.183.0.pdf)
blocking Trump’s order, which prompted the administration to appeal to the
U.S. Supreme Court. Earlier this week, the court’s conservative majority said
Talwani’s move was premature since the executive order had yet to be finalized
into a rule—even though their ruling came days _after_ the Postal Service had
indeed publicly posted its policies for enforcing the sweeping new
restrictions. The court was careful to say it wasn’t addressing the merits of
the issue; still, in her dissent, Justice Jackson said the conservative
justices’ decision creates a “Kafkaesque nightmare” that “risks severe
disruption of the upcoming midterm elections.”  

The Democratic states and the League promptly amended their lawsuits to target
the rule that USPS just issued, and late Thursday Talwani issued a temporary
restraining order that blocks the Postal Service from enforcing it.

This means that, as of publication, USPS cannot refuse to deliver some voters’
mail ballots.

And that’s [likely to stay the
case](https://electionlawblog.org/2026/breaking-the-usps-rule-is-blocked-
again/) for the near future: Talwani has scheduled her next hearing on Sept.
3, shortly before the cycle’s first ballots are scheduled to be mailed out.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/25082793134510-2400x1692.jpg)The disputes around
USPS’s postmark and mail voting rules add to other controversies during the
Trump administration. Here, a labor union protests in 2025 against efforts to
privatize the Postal Service. (Photo by Zach D Roberts/NurPhoto via AP)

  
**“It seems to me that it would be impossible for the USPS to set up a
functional system, much less a fair one, before the November elections to
decide which ballots could and couldn 't be sent. Is this plan even feasible?”
_—  Nancy, from California_**

To be clear, elections experts broadly agree that Trump’s executive order and
the resulting USPS rule is illegal. They also say that, even if the Supreme
Court ends up blessing it and reversing Talwani’s stay, the timing of the
dispute would make it extremely difficult and messy to enforce ahead of the
midterms.

Some states are due to send out mail ballots as soon as early September.

To abide by the order, they’d have to rush to share voter lists with the
federal government in the coming weeks. Preparing lists with the requisite
data would be a huge undertaking for state and local election
officials—particularly now, amid all the other tasks of preparing for the
midterms.

“The voter lists themselves that the states maintain, those took years and
millions of dollars for each state to develop,” said Stewart. “People in all
the state governments will be scrambling over the next couple of weeks to get
the data together, and make sure it's in the right format, and make sure all
this works.”

According to the new USPS rule, the agency intends to launch a web portal to
collect and store voter lists from states. But that portal has not yet been
developed or even piloted at a smaller scale. Even if it launches, said
Charles Stewart, of MIT, there is no guarantee that it will be secure,
functioning, and compatible with each state’s different system for managing
voter rolls.

Plus, local election officials would be hard-pressed to design and obtain new
envelopes that meet the USPS requirements within a matter of days.

Even if states have no time to meet the new mandates, harm would still come if
USPS refuses to deliver ballots in states that don’t comply. But Talwani’s
order this week froze the Postal Service’s authority to do that at a crucial
time, just as states are about to send their first ballots. Justin Levitt, a
voting rights expert and professor at Loyola Law School, is confident that
voters will receive ballots next month due to this timing.

“I think it’s exceptionally likely that by the time we hit mid-September, the
world we live in is a world where ballots are going into voters’ hands and
it’s both too late and not permitted for USPS to do anything with them except
deliver them,” Levitt says. “There’s nothing in the rule that suggests USPS is
claiming the authority to reject ballots coming back in to election officials
in October.”

But Levitt allows that it’s possible that the Supreme Court lifts the judicial
block so quickly that it could allow USPS to try to enforce a non-delivery
policy in the coming weeks.

Plus, most states allow voters to request a mail ballot as late as two weeks
before Election Day, and a hypothetical Supreme Court ruling favoring Trump
later this fall might affect them.

Should the agency regain the authority to implement the order, postal
officials [have said](https://www.notus.org/policy/postal-officials-ballot-
errors) they expect widespread errors.

No matter what happens before November, if the conservative justices end up
siding with Trump, the administration and USPS would then have multiple years
to try to implement their new rules in advance of the 2028 presidential
election. And [recent history](https://boltsmag.org/restrictions-on-grace-
periods-for-mail-ballots/) tells us that many red states, at least, may be
glad to amend their election deadlines in order to match the order.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2025/01/466104990_18463523914004194_6517785059173711743_n-e1737121516271.jpg)Mail
ballots in the Los Angeles County elections’ office in November 2024. (Photo
from LA Clerk's office/Facebook)

  
**“I have voted by mail since the pandemic and it’s been great but what am I supposed to do differently now? Should I stop?” — _Suzie, from Wisconsin_ | “Should people mailing their ballots use drop boxes and avoid the post office in case USPS decides to cave to pressure from Trump and ignore court decisions?” — _@scribunda on bluesky_**

Given that Trump’s executive order is currently suspended, several experts
told _Bolts_ that mail ballots remain a safe and reliable way to vote at this
time.

But they stress that voters in states with postmark deadlines should send in
ballots far ahead of Election Day because of the separate delays in how USPS
postmarks mail. “People should mail their ballots or registration applications
early,” Cohen told _Bolts_.

Voters can also request a postmark from the retail counter at their local post
office to ensure they meet the deadline.

The landscape could still shift in coming weeks, with the possibility that the
U.S. Supreme Court lets Trump implement his order in advance of the midterms.
While experts remain skeptical that USPS can feasibly enforce its new policies
by November, as laid out above, they also say voters should learn about all
the voting options available in their state and [use a guide to make a
plan](https://fairelectionscenter.org/vote-by-mail-guides/) that suits them.

In states that allow early voting, people may have plenty of time to cast
their ballots in person. Many states have secure ballot boxes that allow
people to submit their absentee ballots—if they have already received
them—without relying on the Postal Service. And in some places, voters who
wish to vote from home may be able to print out their ballots themselves (more
on that below).

Voters can call their local elections offices or refer to voter guides to
learn more, Cohen said.

These alternatives are no panacea for voters whose mobility may be impaired or
for whom in-person voting poses a practical difficulty. “The reason that the
administration is attacking mail voting is that it has helped millions of
Americans vote—particularly people who are older, people with disabilities,
people in rural areas that don't live close to an election office,” Cohen
added. “So Americans should exercise that right honestly and in defiance of
the attacks on it.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/20137456204329-2400x1600.jpg)A post office in Isle Au
Haut, Maine. (AP Photo/Robert F. Bukaty)

  
**“As an overseas voter, would I be affected by this USPS list requirement?
How could I even prove my citizenship from here?” _—  @THEScottPHarris on X,
from France_**

Voter participation among overseas American citizens is already much lower
than it is for other American citizens, and the turnout rate would almost
assuredly drop as a consequence of any stricter deadlines for mail-voting
eligibility or added requirements for voter identification.

“Voters that live in our community have a much easier time of coming to our
office in person and providing documentation—birth certificate, driver’s
license, passport,” said Lannie Chapman, the elected clerk of Salt Lake
County, Utah. “It’s a lot more difficult for [overseas voters] to be able to
provide us some of the documentation they might need.”

Mark Lindeman, policy and strategy director of the organization Verified
Voting, told _Bolts_ he remains confident that voter access for overseas
citizens is secure, but he also hesitates to look too far ahead:
“Conceptually, are these proposals threatening to the voting rights of people
overseas? Yeah, absolutely. Do we think these people’s votes are at great risk
in 2026? My current assessment would be no.”

“But,” he added, “that’s cheap talk, because we can’t control what the courts
and Supreme Court do.” (Courts have, so far, [held the
line](https://www.democracydocket.com/news-alerts/gop-targets-u-s-citizens-
living-overseas-in-latest-suppression-scheme/) against [GOP
attacks](https://www.democracydocket.com/news-alerts/nebraska-court-throws-
out-rnc-lawsuit-targeting-overseas-voters/) on overseas voter access.)

Importantly, [overseas voters](https://www.votefromabroad.org/faqs/fwab-what-
is-backup-ballot) have special legal permission to obtain and submit ballots
digitally, and commonly do. This may become a more popular method soon, in the
face of federal threats to mail voting.

The group Democrats Abroad, for one, has lately implored its members to
consider this option: “We strongly encourage voters living abroad to protect
themselves from Donald Trump’s weaponized U.S. Postal Service by going to
[votefromabroad.org](http://votefromabroad.org) and requesting to receive
their ballot by email,” it said in a recent email blast.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/26087435010855-scaled.jpg)A woman takes part in the
"No Kings" protest in Paris, France, in March 2026. (AP Photo/Aurelien
Morissard)

  
**“Do most jurisdictions make you request a mail-in ballot? Do any localities
send one automatically?” _—  Bolts Lover, from Virginia_**

Rules for mail voting vary widely by state, but let’s make this simple by
breaking the country down into three rough categories: all-mail, no-excuse,
and excuse-required.

That first category, all-mail, includes Washington, D.C., and eight
states—California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont, and
Washington—that automatically send all registered voters ballots in the mail
for every election. D.C. [even mails](https://boltsmag.org/washington-dc-bill-
voter-registration/) ballots to residents it has proactively determined are
eligible to vote, even if they're not yet formally registered.

Most of the rest of the country—[29 states, to be
exact](https://ballotpedia.org/All-mail_voting)—falls into the second
category: Any eligible voter can cast a mail ballot, but they need to request
it.

That said, in 10 of those states, people who want to vote by mail only need to
apply once in order to receive mail ballots for subsequent elections. This
status, known as [“permanent absentee”](https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-
campaigns/table-3-states-with-permanent-absentee-voting-lists) voting, keeps
voters from having to ask for their ballot every cycle.

The remainder of states are a lot more strict: They require people to present
[a specific excuse](https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-
campaigns/table-2-excuses-to-vote-absentee), like disability or religious
belief, if they want to vote by mail. This group includes 13 states, mostly in
the South.

States commonly tweak these rules. Connecticut, for instance, was the latest
state to repeal the requirement that mail voters provide an excuse, [with a
law adopted this spring](https://boltsmag.org/connecticut-expands-vote-by-
mail/). Utah, on the other hand, is [sunsetting its all-mail
program](https://boltsmag.org/utah-legislation-ending-universal-vote-by-mail/)
due to growing MAGA hostility against the practice.

To be clear, in all states, voters still have access to some in-person voting
sites if they prefer that method.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/IMG_8111-2400x1600.jpg)A
protest in front of the Utah legislature in 2025 when state Republicans ended
the state's all-mail voting rules (photo courtesy of Bella Brewer/Let Utah
Vote).

  
**“Are there any things the blue states can do to speed up mail delivery and
ensure mail votes are timely like they should be?” — _Mandy_**

Local and state election offices have no control over USPS policy, but the
people who run those offices can and often do take action to try to cut down
delivery times of election mail. Some elections officials personally visit
their local post offices to collect delivered ballots.

“I already go to the post office daily, after we’ve mailed out ballots, to
pick up any returns that they might have for me, instead of waiting for the
post office to bring me those mail ballots,” Chapman, the Salt Lake County
clerk, told _Bolts_. “I go directly to the horse’s mouth and it makes sure
we’re being as efficient as possible.”

State and local governments can also cut down delivery times by expanding
voting opportunities. The more dropboxes and election sites a given area has,
the easier it is for voters to return ballots to election officials while
avoiding USPS entirely, and the lower the chances are that someone’s ballot
return gets slowed down.

States [vary widely](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_drop_box_laws_by_state) in
how much authority they confer upon election officials to expand delivery
opportunities. Arkansas, for example, prohibits dropboxes. Ohio allows only
one ballot dropbox per county. Rhode Island requires every single town to
provide at least one dropbox.

“You can’t force the Postal Service to do anything,” Phil Keisling, the former
Oregon secretary of state, and now a national advocate for mail voting, told
_Bolts_. “But you can make voting convenient. Letting people drop ballots off
at fire stations, city halls, libraries—that’s the kind of thing states can
do, where they have the authority.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Image-from-
iOS-2400x1800.jpg)A ballot drop box in Ann Arbor, Michigan (Photo by Alex
Burness/Bolts)

  
**“I want to know if states like mine (Washington) that only do mail-in voting
have any Plan B? Especially if the USPS does not deliver mail-in ballots, is
there any way that FedEx or UPS could be used?” _— Sarah, from Washington_**

_Bolts_ put this question to several elections officials in all-mail states,
and they all were on alert for if and when USPS is no longer reliable for mail
voters.

“There’s a reason we’re up at 3 a.m., and this is it,” said Chapman, the Salt
Lake County clerk.

“We think about worst-case scenarios,” she said. “We continue to come up with
solutions to what we hope are preposterous hypotheticals.”

Importantly, even all-mail states still do have physical voting systems in
place, meaning that even severe threats to vote-by-mail would not stop most
people from exercising their right to vote. In addition to polling sites and
voting centers, of which most counties have at least one, voters generally
often have lots of choices for returning ballots by dropbox. Washington, for
one, [reports](https://www.sos.wa.gov/elections/voters/voter-
registration/drop-box-and-voting-center-locations) having nearly 600 ballot
dropboxes across its 39 counties. Much tinier Vermont, which is the only all-
mail state in the eastern U.S.,
[reports](https://outside.vermont.gov/dept/sos/Elections_Division/voters/vermont_election_ballot_drop_box_locations.pdf)
more than 250 dropboxes.

If USPS became unreliable for mail voting, Chapman and others said, elections
officials could consider beefing up staffing and operating hours for in-person
polling stations. Officials could also explore contracting with private mail
carriers, though no state currently relies primarily, or even in significant
part, on private carriers for mail ballots.

State and local responses would vary, of course, in the event of significant
future USPS disruption.

“Those scenarios are always being contemplated,” said Keisling, the former
Oregon secretary of state. “Big fire, typhoon, earthquake, you name it. I’m
confident election officials have worst-case scenarios for something as absurd
as the Supreme Court allowing the Postal Service to decide which mail it
delivers.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2025/03/IMG_0378-1-2400x1929.jpg)Salt Lake County Clerk Lannie
Chapman, who runs elections in Utah's most populous counties, says election
officials all over are thinking through contingencies (photo by Alex Burness
for _Bolts_)

  
**“King County, Washington, gives voters the opportunity to print their ballot
online. Does this happen elsewhere? If not, what are the barriers to making
this happen? It seems like the only option that completely bypasses the USPS
(print at home, drop in dropbox).” _—  @kaybee71 on BlueSky_**

This isn’t universal, but it’s more common than you might think.

In King County and elsewhere in Washington, voters who need a fresh
ballot—that includes people whose ballots were lost, stolen, or damaged, or
whose ballots never arrived—can enter their name and date of birth online,
then access their local ballot and print it out for return. [Here’s King
County’s site](https://wa.omniballot.us/sites/53033/site/app/home), for anyone
curious.

The state of Washington was actually
[pushing](https://www.facebook.com/WaSecretaryOfState/videos/if-youre-
affected-by-wildfires-voting-may-not-be-your-top-priority-right-now-
but/1439026971385570/) this option recently, as wildfires ravaged many
communities during the state’s recent primary elections. King County officials
have also [promoted the idea](https://www.kuow.org/2026-07-20/will-trumps-
election-moves-affect-was-primary) as a possible way to guard against USPS
delays.

California also allows all registered voters to print ballots at home, and
then return those ballots in person, in a drop box or by mail. Maryland allows
all registered voters to request a ballot via secure email, which voters can
then print and return.

Still, some voting advocates don’t see this as a panacea in the face of slow
USPS delivery.

Lindeman, an expert on voting systems with Verified Voting, said that ballots
printed at home can be more difficult for state and local vote tabulators to
interpret—a significant potential barrier to expanding the process. For
example, in Maryland, Lindemann said, election officials have to duplicate
home-printed ballots submitted by voters onto pages that the state’s systems
can process.

“You try not to introduce complications unless they’re necessary, and printing
ballots is kind of a Rube Goldberg way to vote,” Lindeman said.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/484543131_1071146675058112_8136453317798095505_n.jpg)King
County, home to Seattle, administers an all-mail voting system (King County
elections/Facebook)

  
**“If mail voting has been used safely by millions of Americans for years,
what’s the actual evidence behind the new restrictions? Are these changes
solving a real problem, or creating new barriers before November?” _—
@ariananiko on BlueSky_**

To hear Trump and allies tell it, their attacks on mail voting are justified
by the fact that mail voting leads to fraud so widespread as to make election
results fundamentally untrustworthy.

But audit after audit and analysis after analysis has found that mail-voting
fraud is exceptionally rare—[literally well under one in a
million](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/mail-voting-in-the-us-data-points-
to-very-low-fraud-and-significant-benefits-to-voters/). Mail voting is
reliable, tested, and increasingly common; [even Trump votes by
mail](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/17/trump-vote-by-mail-primaries-
florida-01039292).

There has been evidence of ballots being delivered to wrong addresses, or to
the address of a deceased person, which is then used to feed conservative
attacks. But even so,[
studies](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/minuscule-number-of-
potentially-fraudulent-ballots-in-states-with-universal-mail-voting-undercuts-
trump-claims-about-election-risks/2020/06/08/1e78aa26-a5c5-11ea-
bb20-ebf0921f3bbd_story.html) and[
investigations](https://docs.wixstatic.com/ugd/ef45f5_81a3affd554e4b5b9b5852f8fb3c10fd.pdf?inline=1)
routinely find that there are vanishingly few instances of actual illegal
voting. States have verification systems to ensure only one ballot from each
person is ever counted,[
using](https://docs.wixstatic.com/ugd/ef45f5_81a3affd554e4b5b9b5852f8fb3c10fd.pdf?inline=1)
signature matching and other measures, including tracking systems with [unique
barcodes](https://verifiedvoting.org/decoding-your-ballot-the-role-of-qr-
codes-and-barcodes/).

But the data tell us something else important: Democrats tend to trust and
utilize vote-by-mail [more
often](https://statesunited.org/resources/americans-vote-by-mail-2024/) than
Republicans. There was not so clear a partisan divide prior to 2020, when
Trump began his crusade against mail ballots, but that year, and in
[2022](https://electionlab.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2023-10/vote-by-
mail.pdf) and
[2024](http://electionlab.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2025-07/HowWeVotedIn2024.pdf),
post-election reports confirmed that Democrats voted by mail much more often,
while Republicans voted more often in person.

This helps explain why Trump and the GOP continue to target mail voting. Their
attack undermines a method Democrats tend to prefer, and makes mail voting a
scapegoat when and where Republicans want to cry foul on election results.
Trump himself has said the quiet part out loud: Mail voting “doesn’t work out
well for Republicans,” [he once
tweeted](https://x.com/realDonaldTrump/status/1247861952736526336). “You’d
never have another Republican elected again,” he said of expanded voter access
generally [in 2020](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2020/03/30/trump-
voting-republicans/).
